unit.title: Behaving properly
unit.goal: Talk about people's behavior in places and under circumstances by choosing and producing modals that match suggestion, obligation, prohibition, permission, or no obligation.

objectiveEvidence.quote: Talk about people’s behavior in places and under circumstances.

prerequisites: will may be recalled only as a contrast; it is not a new focus

focus: should for a suggestion or advice
have to and must for obligation; context can make them overlap
can and can't for permission questions and answers
don't have to for no obligation: the action remains optional
nonGoals: Do not teach have to and must as rigid, mutually exclusive categories.
Do not claim that must is always personal or that have to is always external.
Do not turn an ambiguous photograph into a single graded fact without a stated context.
Do not infer listening answers from an audio URL when a verified transcript is unavailable.

modalMap.note: The speaker presents a helpful or recommended action.

modalMap.example: You have to wear a badge here.
modalMap.note: Often foregrounds a rule, requirement, or responsibility from the situation; must can also express the same obligation.

modalMap.example: I must remember to greet the host.
modalMap.note: Can sound like a strong speaker commitment or requirement; context, not a rigid label, determines the force.

modalMap.example: Can she touch the controls? No, she can't.
modalMap.note: Can ask for permission; can't can deny permission or communicate a prohibition in context.

modalMap.example: The invitation says lunch is provided and bringing your own lunch is optional: You don't have to bring food.
modalMap.note: The action is optional. It does not mean the action is forbidden.

mustnt.example: The sign says No food: You mustn't bring food in.
mustnt.learnerCheck: The speaker cannot choose that action.

dontHaveTo.example: The invitation says lunch is provided and bringing your own lunch is optional: You don't have to bring food.
dontHaveTo.learnerCheck: The speaker may bring food, but it is unnecessary.

pedagogy.sequenceRationale: The eight stages teach the modal meanings before a minimal permission retrieval, use four selected images for focused contextual practice, preserve the remaining source images in the archive, then move to verified listening, form repair, meaning selection, guided role-play, and a real code-of-conduct task.

composition: Use the approved adult semirealistic painterly family, ivory surface, lilac organic decoration, and navy serif headings.
Keep the complete environment and the complete source image in view; use contain for contentful photos and never crop a face or meaningful object.
Each screen has a small unit/status line, one task heading, one short prompt, the actual response area, inline feedback, and one primary footer action.
Keep text short and readable: body at least 16px, heading 32px desktop/26px mobile, spacing from the 8/16/24/32/48px scale, controls at least 44px.
Use a cobalt primary action that changes from Comprobar to Siguiente only after checking; keep Saltar ejercicio as the only footer secondary action.
Wrong clicks leave the answer visible, announce a concise correction, and allow a retry; never use color alone for state.
On mobile, stack media and options in reading order, preserve the full image and keep the footer reachable without horizontal overflow.
visualRequirements.identity: If a new illustration is needed for the host/classroom context, use only the approved Lucas, Carl, or interlocutora identities. Do not assign names or new identities to the source-photo subjects.

Grammar Analysis
Statements Questions Answers
sourceText: Statements Questions Answers 1 You should talk to her. Should I talk to her? Yes, you should talk to her. 2 We have to be nice to them. Do you have to be nice to them? No, we don’t have to be nice to them. 3 She must be careful now. Must she be careful now? No, she mustn't be careful now. 4 They can’t act like children. Can they act like children? Yes, they can act like children.
You should talk to her. / Should I talk to her? / Yes, you should talk to her.
We have to be nice to them. / Do you have to be nice to them? / No, we don’t have to be nice to them.
She must be careful now. / Must she be careful now? / No, she mustn't be careful now.
They can’t act like children. / Can they act like children? / Yes, they can act like children.
We can talk about people’s behaviour and how they are supposed to act by using modals.

To consider 1. All verbs go in simple form after a modal. 2. Modals work with all pronouns with no problem. 3. Modals affect the main verbs according to the speaker's intention. 4. Would is also a common modal; You’ll hear more of it in an upcoming lesson.

sourceRows.title: Language Use
We can use the modals to indicate different meanings in messages.
sourceText: Suggestions: They should not talk loud.
Responsibility: She has to finish his homework.
Obligation: I must act normal before her.
Prohibition: You must not hit your sister. You can’t yell at your mum.

audio.transcript: Man, I'm finally visiting Heather's house. Wait, what? I mean like, having dinner with family? Yes, like that. Oh boy. What should I wear? How am I supposed to act? Calm down. You should act normal, but you must look grateful and honoured. And overall, you must not show that moody side of you. Moody side? Me? Never mind. How about being honoured? Well, you must dress the parents once you are there and tell them how honoured you are for the invitation. Do I have to smile all night? No, there will be hypocrisy, but you need to look happy and you must not ask for more food. What if I'm hungry? You should wait for them to tell you and you should not look hungry, okay? Okay, I will do my best. And you should not be bossy. You are my friend. I'm not bossy. I have a talent for leading people.

scenes.title: Read behavior in context
scenes.purpose: Practice modal force from four explicit written situations. The original source images remain archived for history; the learner interprets the stated rule, advice, prohibition, or invitation instead of guessing a person’s personality.
scenes.instruction: Lee cada situación escrita y elige la frase modal que corresponde. Usa la norma, el consejo o la invitación que aparece en el texto; no adivines la personalidad de nadie.

cards.context: At home, a parent asks a child to tidy up and gives advice about calming down.
cards.modalQuestion: The parent is giving advice, not quoting a rule. What fits?
modalOptions: The child doesn’t have to calm down.
cards.explanation: The parent gives advice, so should fits; mustn’t would prohibit calming down and don’t have to would make it optional.

cards.context: At work, the office handbook requires respectful language when a coworker gives instructions.
cards.modalQuestion: The office handbook requires respectful language. What fits?
modalOptions: Everyone has to use respectful language.
Everyone doesn’t have to use respectful language.
cards.modalAnswer: Everyone has to use respectful language.
cards.explanation: The handbook creates an obligation. Have to is a natural fit for an external rule; must could also express the same requirement.

cards.context: The host says joining the activity is optional; the guest may choose not to join.
cards.modalQuestion: The host says joining is optional. What can the host say?
cards.explanation: Optional means no obligation. Don’t have to leaves the choice open; it does not forbid joining.

cards.context: The class rule says students must not gossip about a classmate during class.
cards.modalQuestion: The class rule forbids gossip. What fits?
modalOptions: They don’t have to gossip in class.
cards.explanation: The stated rule makes gossip prohibited. Mustn’t communicates that prohibition.

interaction.clickCorrection: After a wrong choice, keep the image and response visible; say which meaning to reconsider (suggestion, required, prohibited, or optional) and let the learner try again.
interaction.keyboard: Select the behavior or modal with Enter/Space; no drag is required.

scenes.teacherVariant: Show two selected cards at a time. Ask the learner to explain why the written situation calls for advice, an obligation, a prohibition, or optional action.
scenes.individualVariant: Answer the four selected context cards and write one modal sentence for each. The four archived source images remain reference material; do not turn them into extra practice items or infer pronunciation from them.

runtimeBlocks.content:
Lee la situación antes de elegir. Aquí decides la fuerza del modal, no la personalidad de una persona.

  • should expresa un consejo.
  • have to o must expresan una obligación cuando el contexto la exige.
  • mustn’t indica que una acción está prohibida.
  • don’t have to indica que no es necesario; la acción sigue siendo posible.

Busca la norma, el consejo o la invitación escrita y elige la frase que coincide.

scenes.title: Match force to context
scenes.purpose: Organize modal form, function, and context, including the prohibition/no-obligation contrast.
scenes.ruleText: Use the explicit sign, handbook, invitation, or owner response to decide the force. Mustn’t means prohibited; don’t have to means optional. Have to and must can overlap for obligation when the context supports it.

items.context: The school handbook requires a badge at the door.
items.question: You ___ wear a badge here.
items.explanation: The handbook supplies an external requirement. Must is also possible if the speaker emphasizes the same requirement.

items.context: A friend asks for helpful advice.
items.question: You ___ call her before the meeting.
items.explanation: This is a recommendation, not a ban or a statement that the action is optional.

items.context: A sign says ‘No food in the gallery.’
items.question: You ___ bring food inside.
items.explanation: The sign prohibits the action. Don’t have to would incorrectly make bringing food optional.

items.context: The invitation says lunch is provided and bringing your own lunch is optional.
items.question: You ___ bring food.
items.explanation: The invitation explicitly makes bringing lunch optional. Don’t have to means unnecessary, not forbidden.

items.context: A learner asks permission and the owner denies access to restricted controls.
items.question: Which pair asks for and denies permission to touch the controls?
options: Can she touch the controls? — No, she can’t.
Mustn’t she touch the controls? — No, she shouldn’t.
Doesn’t she have to touch the controls? — No, she doesn’t.
items.correctOption: Can she touch the controls? — No, she can’t.
items.explanation: Can asks for permission and can’t denies permission in this stated situation.

interaction.wrongClick: Show the relevant meaning in words: ‘prohibited’ or ‘not necessary’; do not mark the two as interchangeable.

rows.statement: The posted school handbook says you have to wear a badge here.

items.explanation: The invitation makes bringing food optional, not forbidden.

scenes.title: Listen, then choose the right force
scenes.purpose: Use the verified dinner-visit audio for evidence, then transfer its functions to new contexts.

audio.transcript: Man, I'm finally visiting Heather's house. Wait, what? I mean like, having dinner with family? Yes, like that. Oh boy. What should I wear? How am I supposed to act? Calm down. You should act normal, but you must look grateful and honoured. And overall, you must not show that moody side of you. Moody side? Me? Never mind. How about being honoured? Well, you must dress the parents once you are there and tell them how honoured you are for the invitation. Do I have to smile all night? No, there will be hypocrisy, but you need to look happy and you must not ask for more food. What if I'm hungry? You should wait for them to tell you and you should not look hungry, okay? Okay, I will do my best. And you should not be bossy. You are my friend. I'm not bossy. I have a talent for leading people.

scenes.title: Role-play a house visit
scenes.purpose: Rehearse permission, obligation, prohibition, suggestion, and no obligation in a responsive exchange.
scenes.scenario: You are visiting a friend’s home for dinner. Use the host’s posted or spoken instructions: leave shoes by the door, do not touch the control panel, and wait until the host offers food.

turns.prompt: Ask permission to sit or put your bag somewhere.
turns.model: Can I put my bag here?

turns.prompt: Read the posted house note and state the external rule.
turns.model: You have to leave your shoes by the door.

turns.prompt: Give one helpful suggestion about the visit.
turns.model: You should tell me where to put my coat.

turns.prompt: Read the host’s message and reject touching the controls.
Ask whether bringing food is necessary, then accept the answer.
turns.model: Do I have to bring food? — No, you don’t have to; the host invitation says dinner is provided.

turns.prompt: The host has not invited anyone to eat yet. Respond using the host’s stated instruction.
turns.model: You mustn’t take food yet. You should wait to be told.

successCriteria: Uses can for a permission question and can’t or another clear negative permission response when needed.
Expresses an obligation with have to or must in a clear context; does not claim the forms are always separate.
Expresses a prohibition with mustn’t or can’t.
Expresses no obligation with don’t have to and leaves the action optional.
Responds appropriately to the unexpected behavior and remains intelligible.

teacherVariant.roles: Teacher is the host; learner is the visitor.
teacherVariant.prompts: Show one turn card at a time and recast only the modal or base-form error. Ask ‘Is this forbidden or optional?’ after turns 4 and 5.
teacherVariant.feedback: Teacher-reviewed open response; no automatic pass claim.

individualVariant.roles: Record both voices or alternate visitor and host turns.
individualVariant.supports: Write the six model frames first, then replace the objects and places with a real home or classroom situation.
individualVariant.selfCheck: Underline each modal and label its function before submitting the recording.

interaction.afterRecording: Continue remains available according to the configured recording flow; do not invent a score or attempt count.
interaction.accessibility: Provide the same six prompts as text and a typed response alternative if recording is unavailable.

runtimeBlocks.content:
Visitas a un amigo para cenar. Lee cada turno y graba las dos voces en este orden:

  1. Visitante: Can I put my bag here?
  2. Anfitrión: la nota publicada dice You have to leave your shoes by the door.
  3. Visitante: You should tell me where to put my coat.
  4. Anfitrión: You mustn’t touch the controls.
  5. Visitante: Do I have to bring food? — No, you don’t have to; the host invitation says dinner is provided.
  6. Tarjeta inesperada: aún no te han invitado a comer. Responde: You mustn’t take food yet. You should wait to be told.

Después de leer los seis turnos, graba la conversación y responde a la tarjeta.

runtimeBlocks.instruction: Graba los seis turnos visibles de la visita a la casa y responde a la tarjeta inesperada sobre la comida.

learningModes.individual: Practica y graba las dos voces; usa la alternativa escrita si no puedes grabar.
learningModes.teacher: Alterna visitante y anfitrión con el docente, siguiendo los seis turnos visibles.

reviewChecklist: Pide permiso con Can I put my bag here?
Expresa la nota publicada con You have to leave your shoes by the door.
Prohíbe tocar los controles con mustn’t.
Distingue don’t have to de mustn’t en la pregunta sobre la comida.
Responde a la tarjeta de comida con una prohibición y un consejo.

scenes.title: Make a code for a real visit
scenes.purpose: Transfer the modal system to a usable home-and-school code of conduct and defend the choices in speech.

realTask.situation: You are welcoming a new classmate to a shared study club in a home-like room. Write and present a six-line code whose sources are explicit: a club guide, a posted handbook rule, your own commitment, a host’s instruction, a host invitation, and an invitation that says dinner is provided.
realTask.deliverable: Six written lines totaling the inherited 100–120-word source range, plus a short spoken reading and one response to an unexpected behavior card.
requiredFunctions: one strong obligation or speaker commitment with must
one prohibition with mustn’t or can’t
one can permission question with a negative answer
one don’t have to no-obligation sentence
unexpectedBehaviorCards: A guest reaches for food before the host invites them.
A guest touches the control panel.
A guest speaks loudly while another student is presenting.
realTask.responsePrompt: Choose one card and respond with a prohibition plus a helpful suggestion.
modelAnswer: The club guide suggests: You should speak quietly in the study room.
The posted club handbook says: You have to wear a visitor badge here.
I must remember to greet the host.
The host says: You mustn’t touch the controls.
Can I sit by the window? — No, you can’t; the host’s invitation reserves that seat.
The invitation says dinner is provided, so you don’t have to bring food.
Unexpected card model: The host has not invited us yet. You mustn’t take food before the invitation. You should wait to be told.
contextSources: Host invitation with a reserved seat
Invitation stating that dinner is provided

acceptanceCriteria: Each line names or clearly implies its source context: guide, posted rule, speaker commitment, host instruction, host invitation, or provided meal.
All six required functions appear in a context that makes the force understandable.
Mustn’t is used for an action that is not allowed, while don’t have to leaves an action optional.
Have to and must are treated as overlapping obligation choices where the context allows; no rigid personal-versus-external rule is asserted.
The permission question and negative answer use can/can’t with the base verb.
The learner responds to one unexpected behavior with a clear correction and suggestion.
The spoken reading is intelligible and the written code is readable to a classmate.

teacherVariant.setup: Teacher chooses the study club, a home visit, or a classroom scenario and asks the learner to name the source of two modal choices.
teacherVariant.followUp: Ask ‘Could must also work here?’ for the have-to line, and ‘Is the last action forbidden or optional?’ for the contrast.
teacherVariant.review: Teacher reviews the six functions, context fit, intelligibility, and response to the behavior card.

individualVariant.setup: Choose a real home, school, library, or community setting. State the source of each rule or invitation, draft six lines, record them in two voices, and type the justification for two choices.
individualVariant.support: Use the model frames, then replace only the setting and object nouns. Keep the modal meaning unchanged.
individualVariant.selfCheck: Mark S (suggestion), O (obligation), P (prohibition), Perm (permission), or N (no obligation) beside each line.

rubric.functionFit: 6 points: one for each required function in a clear context
rubric.criticalContrast: 2 points: mustn’t and don’t have to meanings remain distinct
rubric.interaction: 1 point: appropriate response to the unexpected behavior
rubric.formAndIntelligibility: 1 point: modal plus base verb and understandable delivery

assessment.sourceConstraint: The former source requests eight behavior sentences and a 100–120-text opinion. This pilot reduces the sentence count to six functional lines plus one transfer response while retaining the source 100–120-word range for the written deliverable.

interaction.typedAlternative: Always expose the written response field alongside recording.
interaction.feedback: Show teacher feedback beside the response; do not claim a score or automatic mastery.

runtimeBlocks.content:
Producto final: escribe y presenta un código de seis líneas para un club de estudio que recibe a un compañero nuevo. Escribe entre 100 y 120 palabras y deja claro de dónde sale cada idea: guía del club, regla publicada, compromiso propio, instrucción del anfitrión, invitación del anfitrión y comida incluida en la invitación.

Incluye estas funciones:

  • un consejo con should;
  • una obligación con have to o must;
  • una prohibición con mustn’t o can’t;
  • una frase de no obligación con don’t have to;
  • una pregunta de permiso con Can ...? y una respuesta negativa con can’t.

Luego lee el código en voz alta y responde a una tarjeta inesperada con una prohibición y un consejo. No uses una regla general sin indicar su contexto.

runtimeBlocks.prompt: Write six lines (100–120 words) for a real study-club code. Name the source context for each line. Include: one should suggestion; one have to or must obligation; one mustn’t or can’t prohibition; one don’t have to no-obligation statement; and one Can ...? permission question with a can’t negative answer. Then choose one unexpected behavior card and write a prohibition plus a helpful suggestion.
runtimeBlocks.explanation: The written code must show the stated functions and sources; use the typed response for teacher review.

learningModes.individual: Escribe el código con los seis contextos indicados y entrega también tu respuesta a una tarjeta inesperada.
learningModes.teacher: Redacta el código con el docente y explica la fuente de dos líneas antes de entregar.

reviewChecklist: Incluye have to o must para una obligación.
Incluye mustn’t o can’t para una prohibición.
Incluye don’t have to para una acción opcional.
Incluye Can ...? y una respuesta con can’t.
Nombra el contexto de cada línea y responde a una tarjeta inesperada.

runtimeBlocks.instruction: Lee tu código de seis líneas en voz alta y responde a una tarjeta inesperada con una prohibición y un consejo.

learningModes.individual: Graba la lectura y la respuesta a la tarjeta; conserva también el texto escrito.
learningModes.teacher: Lee el código con el docente y responde oralmente a la tarjeta elegida.

reviewChecklist: Lee las seis líneas con sus contextos.
Pronuncia la diferencia entre mustn’t y don’t have to.
Formula la pregunta Can ...? y la respuesta negativa con can’t.
Responde a la tarjeta con una prohibición y un consejo.
